sentences.text: She woke her grandfather in maybe forty seconds.
She said, "Grandpa.
There is a wolf at the north fence and it is hurt and I think it is Ash." Her grandfather did not ask any questions.
He put on his boots and his coat and his heavy snow trousers, and he took the emergency kit from the pantry, and he took a rifle, though he said quietly that it was just in case.
And they went back out into the storm together.
Ash was still there.
She had lain down again in the snow.
She looked up when they came.
She growled, softly, at Kaya's grandfather, but she did not move away.
Kaya's grandfather knelt down slowly, ten meters away.
He said, "Yeah.
Yeah, that is her.
That is her, Kaya.
Look at the mark on her back." He looked at Kaya.
"Good work.
Good work.
Now listen to me.
We need to move very slowly.
If she is scared, this all falls apart."
It took them almost an hour.
Kaya walked in front, holding out her hand, talking softly.
Her grandfather walked behind with a rope and a jacket to throw over Ash's head if they had to.
But Ash followed.
She limped along on three legs, twenty steps and then a rest, twenty steps and then a rest.
Kaya kept talking to her the whole way.
She talked about small things — the storm, the shape of the trees, what she had eaten for supper.
It did not matter what she said.
The tone mattered.
The being with her mattered.
They got Ash into the isolation pen just before three in the morning.
Kaya's grandfather closed the gate.
Ash lay down on the straw.
She did not try to get up.
Her breathing was shallow.
Her grandfather said, "Kaya.
Get me the vet kit.
Get me the light.
Get me the heat lamp.
Move." And they worked.
Her grandfather worked on the leg for two hours.
The injury was not new — maybe two weeks old — and it had gone very bad.
It looked like a snare wound, or a bad break that had not set right.
He cleaned it out.
He gave her something to make her not fight him.
He set the bone.
He wrapped it.
Kaya held Ash's head the whole time, and Ash let her.
She let a stranger touch her injured leg because Kaya was there.
Kaya understood that.
She understood how much trust that was.
When it was done, her grandfather stepped back.
He was very tired.
He said, "She might not make it, Kaya.
I'll be honest with you.
That leg is bad.
She has been out here a long time.
She's underweight.
There is a real chance she does not survive the next few days.
I want you to be ready for that." Kaya said, "I am ready for that." Her grandfather looked at her for a moment.
"You know what," he said.
"You are."
Ash did survive.
It took a long time.
She was in the isolation pen for eight weeks.
Kaya spent almost every day with her — reading books beside her, feeding her, changing her water.
Slowly the leg got better.
It would not be a perfect leg again — she would limp for the rest of her life — but it would work.
She could walk.
She could probably hunt small things, though hunting big things might be hard.
When the road opened in April, they had to decide what to do with her.
Kaya's grandfather sat with her at the kitchen table.
He said, "There are two choices.
We can keep her here.
She could live here safely for the rest of her life.
We would take good care of her.
Or we can release her again, in a place we choose, where she has a chance.
She will not hunt as well as she used to.
But she has proved she is a survivor.
She made it two whole winters.
She might make it many more.
It is your choice, Kaya.
She is your wolf."
Kaya thought about it for three days.
She talked to Ash.
She sat in the pen with her.
She watched her walk.
Then she went to her grandfather and she said, "Release her.
She is a wolf.
She came back because she needed help, and we helped her.
Now she can go again." Her grandfather nodded.
He did not smile, but she could tell he was proud.

So on a morning in late April they drove Ash back up into the mountains, though not as far this time — closer, so she was in country that Kaya knew Ash could get back to the sanctuary from if she ever needed to again.
They opened the crate at the edge of a wide alpine meadow.
Ash stepped out slowly.
She looked back at Kaya.
She held Kaya's eyes for a moment.
Then she turned and she went, limping but real, into the trees.
Kaya watched her go.
She did not cry this time.
She had cried the first time.
This time she just watched, and she smiled a little, and she waved.
Her grandfather said, from behind her, "You did good, kid.
You did really good." And they got in the truck, and they drove home.
